newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle closes in on Russia's Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle closes in on Russia's Mir.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Atlantis cruised on Tuesday toward a linkup with Mir and a change of shift aboard the orbiting Russian outpost.
Atlantis and Mir were due to come together at 10:53 p.m. EST (0353 GMT), as the two craft soared high over Russia, southeast of Moscow. It will be the shuttle's fifth visit to the station.
Soon after the hatches between the craft open, astronaut Jerry Linenger was to take the place of John Blaha, who has worked aboard Mir since September.
The shuttle crew spotted the Russian station against the starry background at about 6:50 p.m. EST (2350 GMT) when they were 51 miles away.
Atlantis and Mir were to remain locked together for five days while the two crews moved a total of 5,975 pounds (2,710 kg) of supplies and equipment between the craft.
Earlier on Tuesday, as the shuttle closed in on Mir, three shuttle astronauts worked out on an experimental treadmill that floated in mid-air like a magic carpet.

NASA wants to use the device aboard the international space station where delicate microgravity experiments can easily be upset by the vibration of exercise. The device employs a complex system of gyroscopes to keep it steady.
It took astronauts Marsha Ivins, Jeff Wisoff and Linenger longer than expected to assemble the device in the orbiter's cramped middeck area, but NASA officials were pleased with the results.
"The system appeared to work," mission operations director Bob Castle told a news conference.
Linenger will be the fourth U.S. astronaut to live aboard Mir as NASA learns to work with Russia before embarking on the international space station project later this year.

"It is incredibe that once two great superpowers who were enemies with nuclear missiles aimed at each other are now holding hands," Blaha told NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin on Tuesday in a telephone call from Mir.
"That's even way beyond science, NASA and space flight as far as the impact that can have on world peace," he said.
Blaha said he had not really missed anything while he was away from earth apart from his wife of 30 years, Brenda.
"I missed my wife," he said. "I hadn't realised how much the separation would hit me."
Blaha is due back to earth on Jan. 22 after 128 days in space.
